notes.meaning: Moses prepares the Israelites in the plains of Moab to renew their covenant with the Lord. A covenant is a sacred agreement between God and his people. This was essentially the same agreement God made at Mount Horeb forty years earlier, but it was now reaffirmed with a new generation about to enter the promised land.

differ.view: This passage introduces a distinct covenant concerning the land and a future changed heart, rather than just a renewal of the covenant made at Sinai.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: In the Hebrew Bible, this verse is counted as the final verse of chapter 28, acting as the closing summary of the previous blessings and curses rather than the start of a new speech.

notes.meaning: Moses calls the whole nation together and reminds them of the astonishing wonders God performed in Egypt. Even those who were children at the time had seen or known of the plagues brought against Pharaoh and his land. God displayed his unmatched power through these signs to show that he alone is the true God and rescuer of his people.

Even though the people had seen great miracles with their physical eyes, they still lacked true spiritual understanding. Simply witnessing wonders does not change the human heart or create faithful obedience on its own. True insight into God's ways is a gift from God that requires a willing and humble heart.

differ.view: Spiritual sight and a receptive heart are sovereign gifts of God's special grace, without which fallen human beings cannot understand divine truth.
God would have given the people understanding if they had sincerely asked, so their lack of spiritual sight was entirely their own fault.

notes.meaning: God speaks directly to remind Israel of his miraculous care during their forty years in the wilderness. Their clothes and sandals never wore out, and they were fed with food from heaven rather than ordinary bread and wine. God provided for them in this supernatural way so they would learn to depend completely on him as their Lord.

Moses recounts their recent victories over King Sihon and King Og when those rulers attacked Israel. The Lord enabled Israel to defeat them and take their land east of the Jordan River. That fertile ground was given as an inheritance to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, proving that God was already fulfilling his promises.

In light of all the great things God had done, Moses urges the people to obey every word of this covenant. Faithfully following God's commands was the only sure way for them to prosper and act wisely in everything they did. Remembering God's past help gives believers strong confidence to obey him in the present.

The entire assembly stands together before the Lord to enter the covenant. This crowd included tribal leaders, elders, officers, ordinary men, women, and little children. It even included foreign residents doing hard camp labor, like chopping wood and carrying water, showing that every member of the community was included in God's promises.

The people assembled to enter the Lord's covenant and accept its binding oath. By this act, God confirmed them as his own chosen people and pledged to be their God, just as he had promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Stepping into this relationship was a serious commitment that brought both God's rich blessing and accountability to his law.

Moses makes it clear that this covenant bound more than just the crowd standing before him that day. It also applied to any Israelites absent from the assembly, as well as future generations who were not yet born. Just as a royal charter binds a family and their descendants, the covenant passed down both privileges and duties to their children.

Moses reminds the people of what they witnessed during their long stay in Egypt and their journey past other nations. They saw the repulsive false gods worshipped by those peoples, carved out of wood, stone, silver, and gold. Calling these idols detestable was a warning to keep Israel from being lured into copying the empty religions of their neighbors.

The leaders are told to watch carefully so that no individual, clan, or tribe turns their heart away from the Lord to worship idols. Turning from God to false gods is compared to a hidden root that sprouts poisonous, bitter weeds. If secret compromise is allowed to take root, its toxic fruit will eventually corrupt and ruin the entire community.

Moses warns against anyone who hears the curses of the covenant and falsely reassures himself that he will be safe. Such a person thinks he can stubbornly follow his own evil desires without facing any consequences from God. That kind of arrogant attitude spreads ruin everywhere, destroying both the fertile ground and the dry.

The Lord will refuse to forgive anyone who clings to such stubborn rebellion. Instead, God's anger and jealousy will burn against that person, bringing every curse written in this book upon him until his very name is wiped out. God will single out the unrepentant sinner from all the tribes as a clear example of divine justice.

Future generations of Israelites and travelers from distant lands would see the terrible judgments fallen on the country. The land would become a barren wasteland of salt and burning sulfur where no crops or grass could grow. Its destruction would look just like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, which God wiped out in his fierce anger because of their wickedness.

People from surrounding nations would look at the desolate country and ask why the Lord had struck it with such furious wrath. The answer would be widely known: the people had abandoned the covenant of the Lord, who had delivered their ancestors out of Egypt. The ruined land would stand as public proof of what happens when a nation breaks faith with God.

The people brought disaster on themselves by bowing down to foreign gods that had never helped them and that God had never appointed for them to serve. Because of their idolatry, the Lord's burning anger unleashed every curse written in this book against their land. In great wrath and indignation, he uprooted Israel from their home and threw them into exile in a foreign land.

God has hidden plans and purposes that belong only to him, which human beings cannot fully know or understand. At the same time, he has openly revealed his laws and promises so that his people and their children may obey them forever. Rather than worrying about secret things, believers are called to focus on living out what God has clearly commanded.

differ.view: This passage highlights the difference between God's secret will, which ordains everything that happens, and his revealed will in Scripture, which teaches believers how they ought to live.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some older translations read the verse as a single thought, meaning that the things once hidden with the Lord have now been made manifest to believers and their children.
